result.question: What should a dynasty fantasy football manager monitor and act on, in priority order and by frequency, according to the most respected dynasty strategy sources (Dynasty League Football, Dynasty Nerds, KeepTradeCut's blog/podcast, DynastyProcess, r/DynastyFF canon, established dynasty analysts) — and how does that priority order differ between (a) a REBUILDING team vs. a CONTENDING team, and (b) off-season vs. in-season? Context: a 12-team Superflex PPR dynasty league, single team, currently rebuilding, checked daily each morning. I need a prioritized ladder of the manager's recurring questions/decisions (e.g., player value drift, buy/sell window timing, rookie pick accumulation and rookie eval, age-curve exits, roster construction rules, taxi/waiver churn, trade partner scanning) with: importance ranking per phase, natural check frequency for each (daily/weekly/monthly), and what evidence/metrics each question needs in front of the manager to be answered well. Cite sources; where strategists disagree, note the disagreement.
result.summary: The sources converge on a phase-dependent monitoring ladder for a rebuilding 12-team Superflex PPR manager. Daily: player value drift on Superflex-specific market values (KTC recalculates continuously with every submission, so day-to-day movement is real) — used as a gut check, not a verdict — plus, during the April–May rookie-draft window, rookie ADP, which moves at daily frequency. Weekly: league-wide supply/demand scanning (which contenders need what, which rival rebuilders are selling the same asset type) to time sells, and in-season specifically, buying rookie picks from struggling contenders when picks are at their annual price floor and flipping stashed backup QBs who inherit starting jobs. Monthly/seasonal: age-curve exit audits (each young asset's age relative to rookie-contract expiry, on a 2–3 year projection horizon), the pre-rookie-draft reconciliation of pick count against droppable roster spots, and the offseason-planned initiation of any rebuild or teardown. The rebuild/contend flip is the clearest consensus in the corpus: rebuilders prioritize volume of pick capital and high-variance swings while selling anything unlikely to contribute to a title one-plus years out; near-contenders invert to consolidation, packaging late capital into earlier picks and specific player targets — with a live disagreement about how far pick accumulation should go (PFF's "more picks, more shots" vs. Dynasty Nerds' warning that hoarding beyond roster capacity and overvaluing picks relative to proven young talent are rebuild-killing traps).

findings.claim: Player market value is a genuine daily-frequency signal, and for this league it must be the Superflex value set specifically: KTC recalculates values in real time with every user submission (so drift changes day to day), and its Superflex and 1QB databases are computed entirely independently — even non-QB values differ between formats. KTC itself instructs managers to treat its calculator as a gut check, not an authoritative verdict, because trade value is owner-, team-, and situation-specific.
findings.evidence: Primary source, three verbatim-verified passages: "Every time someone submits a KTC the rankings are updated"; "Our Superflex and One QB databases operate entirely independently of one another... which is why there can sometimes be differences between the two even for non-QBs"; "trading is so owner, team, and situation specific that calculators are at best a gut check." Corroborated by KTC's daily risers/fallers feature and third-party real-time KTC alert services. Merges claims 0, 1, 2 (all 3-0).

findings.claim: The dynasty trade calendar is seasonal and predictable, and it drives the rebuilder's in-season vs. off-season task split: rookie picks are cheapest in-season (buy them then, especially from injured/collapsing contenders) and most expensive in the offseason and right before the rookie draft (sell picks then, ideally on or near draft day); overperformers sell immediately while optimism is high, before the NFL Draft and free agency deflate them; aging veterans sell once the season begins and contenders need help. Pick-market timing therefore has action points in BOTH phases — buy windows in-season, sell windows at the draft.
findings.evidence: PFF (verified verbatim): "Most managers overpay for picks in the offseason or right before the rookie draft... the best time to acquire rookie picks? During the season... They're abstract. They don't score points." Fantasy Life (verified): sell overperformers "pronto while optimism is still high"; sell picks "as close to your league's rookie draft as possible. On the day, if possible." Independently corroborated by Adam Harstad at Footballguys ("buy during the season, sell during the draft"). Merges claims 4 (2-1) and 17 (3-0). Note: a harder variant pinning the buy window to Sept–Nov and sell window to Feb–Apr was REFUTED (1-2) — the direction of the cycle is consensus, the exact month boundaries are not.

findings.claim: A rebuild should be initiated in the NFL offseason as a pre-planned process, not improvised in September or at the November trade deadline — selling under time pressure fails to extract full value because buying leverage evaporates as playoffs approach.
findings.evidence: RotoWire (Jerry Donabedian, updated 2026-06-03), verified verbatim: "It's nearly impossible to extract full value for assets if we're determined to sell them off as fast as possible... we'd ideally start our rebuilding process during the NFL offseason as a pre-planned thing." Corroborated by Dynasty Nerds deadline coverage (sellers accept below perceived value at the deadline). Single named-analyst source and a 2-1 vote; the source says "ideally," softer than "should."

findings.claim: Rebuild asset doctrine: prioritize volume of draft capital and high-variance upside swings over early consolidation ("take swings; draft guys who could blow up") — but this is bounded by two named traps: (a) do not hoard picks beyond roster capacity, and (b) do not overvalue speculative picks relative to proven young talent, because trading an established young player for picks can halt a rebuild outright. This is a genuine documented disagreement: PFF/consensus says volume; Dynasty Nerds says quality-over-quantity past a point; DynastyProcess's own pick model exists because managers systematically overrate rookie hit rates.
findings.evidence: PFF verified: rebuilders should focus on "acquiring more picks and more shots and more time... Take swings" and "Don't rush to consolidate those picks too early." Fantasy Life verified: "I've seen people completely halt a solid rebuild attempt by sending away the next Randy Moss for the chance to draft another Randy Miss." Dynasty Nerds names pick-overloading a rebuild trap. Verifiers found broad multi-source agreement on the volume principle (FTN, RotoWire, Fantasy Points, The Undroppables) with the qualification carried forward. Merges claims 5 and 18 (both 3-0).

findings.claim: The priority order flips as the team nears contention: stop accumulating and consolidate — package late-round pick capital into earlier picks and specific player targets to accelerate the window. This is the single cleanest rebuild-vs-contend difference in the corpus; the only live debate is the size of the consolidation premium, not its direction.
findings.evidence: PFF verified verbatim: near-contention teams "should start thinking about player targets, packaging late-round capital into earlier picks and preparing to turn draft picks into production," explicitly contrasted with rebuilders prioritizing volume. KTC's calculator encodes the same consolidation premium ("four quarters don't equal a dollar"), and real-trade data (RosterAudit) shows managers pay it.

findings.claim: Rebuilding rosters should not be rookies-and-picks-only: managers should speculate on veterans specifically to create future trade chips, evaluate players on a 2–3 year production window and current lineup usability, and keep some proven producers to "ride until they are done." The sell rule that governs the roster audit: trade away anyone unlikely to contribute to a championship roughly one year out (overperformers, twilight veterans, peaked short-horizon contributors). Note the tension between the aggressive one-year prune rule (Fantasy Life) and the hold-proven-production stance (Dynasty Nerds) — strategists disagree on how bare a rebuild roster should run.
findings.evidence: RotoWire verified: rookies-only "isn't a realistic dynasty league strategy"; rebuilders "speculate on value in anticipation of trading the player for something else (often picks)." Dynasty Nerds verified (via Wayback — live URL moved): "Can this player be productive for your team in the next two or three years?... Don't be afraid to acquire some proven talent who you might ride until they are done." Fantasy Life verified: "If they're unlikely to help win a championship a year from now, prune 'em." Merges claims 3, 13, 16 (all 3-0). Verifiers softened RotoWire's "must" to "should" and noted the one-year horizon is one author's framing.

findings.claim: Age-curve management is a standing (roughly monthly) question, not a one-time filter: prioritize age over NFL experience when acquiring (a 22-year-old sophomore over a 24-year-old rookie; drafted rookies ideally under 22), continuously monitor each young asset's age at rookie-contract expiry and the strength of the free-agency class he will compete against ("recently drafted" ≠ "long career ahead"), and cap value projection at a 2–3 year horizon — Dynasty Nerds holds that fantasy value cannot be reliably projected further due to roster turnover, injury, and free agency (with a QB exception relevant to Superflex).
findings.evidence: All three passages verified verbatim (claims 8, 14, 19; all 3-0). Corroboration: PlayerProfiler breakout-age data (WR breakout age <19 → ~69% top-36 hit rate vs >21 → ~10%); PFF/Apex RB age-curve data (~57–68% of top-24 RB production at ages 23–26). Disagreement noted by verifiers: Adam Harstad (Footballguys mortality tables) rejects rigid cliff framing in favor of probabilistic career length, and the 2–3-year article itself excepts QBs (Rodgers/Stafford/Wilson retained value) — material for Superflex QB planning. A harder companion claim (QB1 must be aged 21–30) was REFUTED 0-3.

findings.claim: Position-specific buy/sell heuristics that require ongoing value-drift monitoring: for RBs — sell aging backs to contenders before the cliff, buy the dip on undervalued young backs in temporarily bad situations, and acquire RBs via rookie drafts (because RBs peak early and decline with little warning); for WRs — target 2nd/3rd-year receivers who are producing or show upside and acquire them BEFORE their value spikes, while treating veteran WRs as tradeable value but never core assets. The WR rule is rebuild-phase advice; contender guidance points the opposite way (buy discounted veteran WRs).
findings.evidence: Both passages verified verbatim (claims 20, 21; both 3-0): RBs "peak early and decline quickly, sometimes even falling off a cliff with little warning" with the three named pivots (Henry sell, Benson dip-buy, rookie-draft investment); WR targets are "2nd- or 3rd-year players... before their value spikes," with Adams/Evans/Hill "not... your core assets." Single-outlet (Dynasty Nerds, July 2025, named author, part of a series); verifiers flagged the RB-cliff premise as qualified by Harstad and by Henry/Barkley's late-career seasons, and marked the WR heuristic as phase-dependent.

findings.claim: The rookie draft window (post-NFL-draft, early May) is the peak event of the dynasty offseason regardless of class strength, and it imposes two specific monitoring behaviors: (a) rookie ADP becomes a daily-frequency signal in April–May (Footballguys refreshes rookie ADP daily in-app during this window, and landing spots swing values within days), and (b) BEFORE the draft, reconcile rookie-pick count against droppable roster spots and consolidate via trade if picks exceed drop candidates — otherwise post-draft cuts force selling assets at a discount.
findings.evidence: Footballguys (Dan Hindery, 05/04/2026) verified: "rookie draft week is still the highlight of the dynasty offseason" even in "arguably the weakest rookie skill position group" in a decade; "The rookie draft ADP in the app will continue to update daily." Dynasty Nerds verified verbatim including the consequence: "...have to sell someone at a discount because you would rather get something over nothing." Merges claims 10 (2-1), 11 (3-0), 12 (3-0). Caveat from the split vote: daily ADP refresh is documented fact, but "because it's volatile" was the claimant's inference, not the source's statement.

findings.claim: Superflex-specific rebuild play: stash backup quarterbacks specifically to flip them in-season to QB-needy contenders once they inherit starting jobs — routinely returning third-round and occasionally second-round picks. This is an in-season sell-window activity that lands on the rebuild side because contenders are structurally the buyers.
findings.evidence: RotoWire verified verbatim: "In superflex or two-QB leagues, backup quarterbacks can also become weekly fantasy starters... mostly the idea is to sell these guys in-season to other teams who are looking to plug weaknesses... a way to pick up third-round picks, or occasionally even a second-rounder." Corroborated by FantraxHQ and The Devy Royale. Verifier caveat: contenders also stash backup QBs (for bye/injury coverage), so the stash itself isn't phase-exclusive — the flip-for-picks is.

findings.claim: Before any veteran sale, scan the entire league for supply and demand: identify rival rebuilders shipping the same asset type (a competing seller at your position drives your return down) and map contenders' specific positional needs so your supply meets a named demand. This makes trade-partner scanning a recurring weekly-ish task that precedes, not follows, the decision to sell.
findings.evidence: Verified verbatim including the causal mechanism: "If you are both trying to peddle your veteran quarterback, that probably drives the cost down if there is only one team looking to acquire a quarterback for a championship run... Look around the league and see what the demand is. Are there teams that are close but need wide receivers?" Single blog source (though Dynasty Nerds is a named respected outlet in the research question); no contradicting source found, adjacent sources reinforce the premise.

result.caveats: Source-tier gap: several of the research question's named canonical sources are thin or absent in the surviving evidence — no direct DLF strategy claims survived, DynastyProcess appears only as corroboration, and r/DynastyFF canon appears only via verifier cross-checks; much of the ladder rests on Dynasty Nerds (one respected outlet, but blog-tier, and one key article now 404s at its original URL — cite the Wayback capture or the moved /dynasty/ path) plus RotoWire, PFF, Footballguys, and Fantasy Life (not a named top-tier source). Frequency assignments (daily/weekly/monthly) are largely inferred from data-update cadences (KTC real-time, Footballguys daily ADP) and seasonal windows rather than explicitly prescribed check schedules — no source hands down a literal daily checklist. Two findings rest partly on 2-1 votes (rebuild-in-offseason; pick-buy timing), and three harder variants were refuted outright (the four-archetype veteran list, the QB1 age-21–30 rule, and the exact Sept–Nov buy / Feb–Apr sell month windows) — so precise numeric boundaries in this space are unreliable even where directional principles are consensus. Time sensitivity: KTC mechanics and the 2026 articles are current as of July 2026, but ADP/value specifics and player examples (Henry, Benson, Nacua) date quickly; the strategic calendar itself is evergreen. Two genuine strategist disagreements should survive into any product framing: pick volume vs. quality-over-quantity in rebuilds, and hard age-cliff framing vs. Harstad's probabilistic career-length view.
openQuestions: What is the contending team's in-season priority ladder? The surviving evidence covers the rebuild phase far more densely; contender guidance appears only by inversion (consolidate, buy veteran WRs, be the pick-seller's counterparty) and was never directly sourced.

What do respected sources actually prescribe for Superflex QB age-curve management? The specific QB1 age 21–30 rule was refuted 0-3, and the 2–3-year-horizon article explicitly excepts QBs — leaving the highest-value position in this league format without a verified exit-timing rule.

Taxi-squad and waiver-churn strategy — explicitly part of the research question — produced no surviving claims at all; what cadence and criteria do dynasty sources prescribe for taxi promotions/poach protection and speculative waiver adds?

How large is the consolidation premium a near-contender should pay when packaging picks up? The direction is consensus (KTC's 'four quarters don't equal a dollar'), but the magnitude is disputed and unquantified in the surviving evidence.

refuted.claim: Rebuilding teams should prioritize four specific veteran acquisition archetypes: very young non-rookies, handcuffs, late-breakout candidates, and buried players who could gain value via a real-life trade.

The recommended age-curve rule for quarterbacks (directly relevant to Superflex): your QB1 should be aged 21-30, while older QBs (e.g., Rodgers, Stafford, Wilson at time of writing) are only acceptable as QB2 depth — not core assets.
Rookie picks should be bought during the in-season months (September–November) when contenders undervalue them, and sold in February–April when offseason hype maximizes their return.
